Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
A specific temperature on the skin

repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

vignette: Amir's hands moved deftly over the fabric, his fingers instinctively knowing the intricate patterns and textures that would bring his designs to life. But even as he worked, his mind wandered back to that day - the sound of crumbling concrete, the acrid smell of smoke, and the feeling of being trapped. The memory was never far away, and when it surfaced, Amir's body responded with a wave of nausea and a sudden sensitivity to temperature changes. He would feel a chill run down his spine, as if the air conditioning in his studio had kicked into overdrive. When these triggers hit, Amir would try to push them away by throwing himself into his work. He'd take on more projects than he could handle, just to keep his mind occupied and his hands moving. But at night, when the studio was quiet and he was alone with his thoughts, he'd find himself checking the locks over and over again - a habit that had started as a way to feel safe but now felt like a compulsion. He'd also begun to hurt himself physically, scratching his skin until it bled, in an attempt to release the overwhelming feelings of anxiety that threatened to consume him. As he navigated the city streets, Amir's eyes would constantly scan for signs of danger - a suspicious package, an unattended car, or a person lurking in the shadows. He'd always identify escape routes before entering a building or public space, just in case. His friends and family had begun to notice his constant vigilance, but Amir couldn't shake the feeling that he was living on borrowed time. When memories of the event flooded back, they came in disconnected pieces - the sound of sirens, the feel of dust in his lungs, and the taste of smoke on his tongue. The vividness of these memories made it hard for Amir to concentrate on anything else. He'd find himself zoning out in meetings or staring blankly at his designs, unable to focus. But even as he struggled to piece together what had happened that day, Amir's memories seemed to be shifting and changing. They felt present, not past - like the event was still unfolding before him. This feeling of timelessness made it hard for him to distinguish between what was real and what was just a memory. His mind would spiral back into the disaster, reliving the fear and panic all over again. The more Amir tried to avoid these memories, the more they seemed to haunt him. He'd see things out of the corner of his eye - movement where there wasn't any, or shapes that didn't quite add up. And when he couldn't shake the feeling that something was off, he'd find himself back at square one - checking locks, scanning for danger, and trying to escape. It was a cycle Amir couldn't seem to break, no matter how hard he tried. His friends and family had encouraged him to seek help, but Amir was afraid of what would happen if he let his guard down - even for a moment. He knew that the memories and triggers were still out there, waiting to pounce. But with each passing day, it felt like the walls were closing in around him.
